newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: Malaysia finds new tyre material for rubber - report.
newsitem.headline: Malaysia finds new tyre material for rubber - report.

text.p: Malaysia has found a new material to shorten the process of making tyres that will create more demand for its natural rubber, the national Bernama news agency reported.

The new technology, using a material called "carbon master batches", will help the country export more value-added rubber and less latex, Bernama quoted Primary Industries Minister Lim Keng Yaik as telling a news conference in Ipoh, northern Malaysia, on Sunday.

Lim said Malaysia was also trying to convince Thailand and Indonesia -- the world's two largest rubber producers -- to also adopt the technique, which he said will create better prices for natural rubber from the region.
Carbon master batches are a processed form of latex, the milky fluid from rubber trees, which is the raw material for most tyres.
"This is part of our new marketing strategy to get a fair and remunerative price (for rubber), unlike now where the prices are decided by consuming countries," Lim said.
A spokesman for the Primary Industries Ministry said on Monday that further research and development was needed.
Rubber traders said they did not expect much impact on prices from the Malaysian initiative.

"Any discovery is going to take time to develop and we can't say for certain whether there will be more uses found for synthetic rubber in the meantime to counter this new technology," said a trader in Kuala Lumpur.
Another dealer said the value of the new product could only be ascertained when it reached the market.
"We'll have to see whether it really cuts short the process of making tyres and is not going to need more work and time in the factories," said the dealer.
Lim said at the opening of a global rubber meeting last week that natural rubber prices have been suppressed for too long and he urged major tyre manufacturers to support reasonable prices.

"If there is no fair remunerative price for rubber, then producers will be forced to cut back on production and rubber prices will spiral like nobody's business," he warned before the start of the International Natural Rubber Organisation meeting.
